raw_response:
I’m an old hand at this, so I won’t make big changes unless there is a clear reason. My land is only 16.9 mu, and with some people working off-farm, I have to keep the work timely and the spending steady. For wheat, I will do about what has worked on my fields before: sow in early October, use a decent local improved seed, put most fertilizer down as base, then watch the color of the crop and topdress once at jointing. Wheat is the crop I don’t want to starve, because if it gets weak over winter it is hard to recover. I have well water, but pumping costs money, so I will irrigate mainly at the key stages, not too many times unless spring is dry.

For summer maize, the main thing is speed after wheat harvest. In our place the turnaround is tight, so I won’t do fancy tillage. I will harvest wheat, clear the field quickly, and plant maize right away. Maize usually follows the wheat fertilizer effect a bit, so I don’t need to be too heavy, but I also don’t want to cut too much and risk yield. I’ll use hybrid maize seed, apply base fertilizer plus one topdress around the big bell-mouth stage, and irrigate only if the rain does not come when the crop is forming ears. This way I keep the double-cropping system stable, don’t spend too much cash at once, and rely on what I’ve seen work here for many years.
